title: What are Compact Object Headers (JEP 519, Java 25) — shrinking the per-object header (mark word + class pointer) from ~96/128 bits toward 64 bits — and why does a smaller header reduce heap footprint and GC pressure for allocation-heavy workloads with many small objects?

s1_definition.profdef: Compact Object Headers, delivered as JEP 519 and made a product feature in Java 25, shrink the fixed per-object header that the HotSpot JVM stamps on every heap object. Traditionally the header is a mark word plus a class pointer, which is about ninety-six bits with compressed class pointers or one hundred twenty-eight bits without. Compact headers fold the class-pointer information into the mark word so the header collapses toward sixty-four bits, which is eight bytes. Because every object pays this header, trimming it saves memory and reduces garbage-collection work across allocation-heavy workloads dominated by many small objects.
s1_definition.analogy: Every cheque that National Bank of India prints has a fixed printed border at the top, the logo, the branch code, and a watermark, before any actual amount is written. That fixed border is the object header. If each cheque carries a sixteen-byte border and the bank prints hundreds of millions of cheques a day, the border alone wastes a huge amount of paper. Compact Object Headers are like redesigning that border to fit in eight bytes while still carrying the logo and branch code. Each individual cheque saves only a little, but across hundreds of millions of cheques the bank saves truckloads of paper, and the sorting machines, which are the garbage collector, have less to move.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compact Object Headers squeeze the mark word and class pointer into a single eight-byte header, so every small object shrinks and the garbage collector copies less.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Compact Object Headers, delivered as JEP 519 and made a product feature in Java 25, shrink the fixed per-object header that the HotSpot JVM stamps on every heap object. Traditionally the header is a mark word plus a class pointer, which is about ninety-six bits with compressed class pointers or one hundred twenty-eight bits without. Compact headers fold the class-pointer information into the mark word so the header collapses toward sixty-four bits, which is eight bytes. Because every object pays this header, trimming it saves memory and reduces garbage-collection work across allocation-heavy workloads dominated by many small objects.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Every cheque that National Bank of India prints has a fixed printed border at the top, the logo, the branch code, and a watermark, before any actual amount is written. That fixed border is the object header. If each cheque carries a sixteen-byte border and the bank prints hundreds of millions of cheques a day, the border alone wastes a huge amount of paper. Compact Object Headers are like redesigning that border to fit in eight bytes while still carrying the logo and branch code. Each individual cheque saves only a little, but across hundreds of millions of cheques the bank saves truckloads of paper, and the sorting machines, which are the garbage collector, have less to move.

**One line to remember:** Compact Object Headers squeeze the mark word and class pointer into a single eight-byte header, so every small object shrinks and the garbage collector copies less.

sections.s2_technical:
Every object on the Java heap begins with a header that the JVM uses internally, before any of your own fields. That header has two parts. The mark word holds runtime bookkeeping such as the identity hash code once computed, the biased or lightweight locking state, and the age bits the garbage collector uses to decide when to promote an object. The class pointer, often called the klass pointer, points to the metadata that describes the object's class, which the JVM needs for method dispatch, type checks, and field layout. On a sixty-four-bit JVM the mark word is eight bytes, and the class pointer is four bytes when compressed class pointers are on or eight bytes when they are off, giving a total header of twelve or sixteen bytes.

For a large object with many fields, twelve or sixteen bytes of header is negligible. The problem is the opposite case: workloads that allocate enormous numbers of small objects. Think of a trading system creating one small event object per tick, or a cache holding hundreds of millions of tiny key-value nodes. If each object holds only a few bytes of real data but carries a sixteen-byte header, the header can dominate the footprint. The header tax is paid once per object, so it scales with object count, which is exactly where small-object workloads hurt.

Compact Object Headers address this by reorganizing the header so the class information is encoded within the mark word rather than stored as a separate full pointer. The result is a header that can be just eight bytes. This is enabled with the flag `-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`. In Java 25 this moved from an experimental flag to a product feature under JEP 519, meaning it is supported for production use rather than being gated behind unlock flags.

The two benefits follow directly. First, footprint drops. Every object is smaller by up to eight bytes, and for a heap full of small objects that can be a double-digit percentage reduction in live-set size, which means you can either hold more objects in the same heap or run the same workload in a smaller heap. Second, garbage-collection pressure drops. A copying or compacting collector physically moves live objects during collection, and the cost of moving is proportional to the bytes moved. Smaller objects mean fewer bytes to copy on every young-generation collection, shorter pause times, and less memory bandwidth consumed. There is also a cache-locality win: more objects fit in each CPU cache line, so field access can be faster.

The senior-level nuance is that the benefit is highly workload-dependent. A service dominated by a few large arrays sees almost nothing, because the header is a tiny fraction of each array. A service that allocates billions of small objects, which is common in event processing, JSON parsing, and fine-grained caches, can see a meaningful heap reduction. You measure it, you do not assume it. You also validate interactions with features that use the mark word, such as identity hash codes and locking, because those bits now share tighter space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a real-time transaction-enrichment pipeline that creates one small immutable event object for every card swipe, and on a busy day that is hundreds of millions of tiny objects. The service runs hot on garbage collection, with frequent young-generation pauses, even though each event carries only a few bytes of real data. This is exactly how object headers work: the fixed header on each tiny event dominates its footprint, so the collector copies far more bytes than the business data would suggest.

Problem 2 — The platform team wants to know, before upgrading to Java 25 and enabling compact headers, how much heap and copy-work they would save, because the win depends entirely on how small the objects are. This is exactly how Compact Object Headers help: the smaller the per-object payload, the larger the percentage saved by trimming the header from sixteen bytes toward eight.

We will build a runnable demo that models a tiny SwipeEvent object, estimates its footprint under a traditional sixteen-byte header versus a compact eight-byte header, computes the total heap and per-GC copy savings across a large event count, and logs the result. The code includes a SwipeEvent domain object, a HeaderModel that reports header size for a given mode, a FootprintCalculator that computes per-object and aggregate bytes, and a demo main that compares traditional and compact modes for one hundred million events.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build (Java 25 toolchain)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with TRADITIONAL headers
java -XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders -jar target/swipe-enrichment-service-1.0.0.jar

# Run with COMPACT headers (product feature in Java 25, JEP 519)
java -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders -jar target/swipe-enrichment-service-1.0.0.jar

# Inspect real object layout to confirm header size (JOL tool)
java -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders -cp jol-cli.jar org.openjdk.jol.Main internals com.bank.enrich.SwipeEvent
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one hundred million SwipeEvent objects, each carrying eight bytes of real payload.

Step 1: The HeaderModel reports the traditional header as twelve bytes and the compact header as eight bytes.

Step 2: The FootprintCalculator adds the header to the eight-byte payload. Traditional is twelve plus eight equals twenty, rounded up to twenty-four bytes for alignment. Compact is eight plus eight equals sixteen bytes, already aligned.

Step 3: Multiplying by one hundred million, the traditional layout needs about 2288 megabytes, while the compact layout needs about 1525 megabytes.

Step 4: The calculator computes the saving as the difference over the traditional total, which is about thirty-three percent.

Step 5: Because that exceeds twenty percent, the demo logs a warning explaining the saving is large precisely because the events are tiny and the header dominated.

Step 6: The same percentage applies to garbage-collection copy work, because a copying collector moves bytes, and there are one-third fewer bytes to move on every young-generation collection.

```
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Traditional headers        (header = 12 bytes)
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Compact Object Headers ON  (header = 8 bytes, JEP 519 / Java 25)
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Traditional heap for 100000000 events: 2288 MB
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Compact heap for 100000000 events:     1525 MB
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Heap AND per-GC copy saving: 33.3%
2026-10-30 17:46:10 WARNING Large saving because events are TINY — header dominated the object.
2026-10-30 17:46:10 INFO    Sample swipe amount (paise): 245050
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  100,000,000 tiny SwipeEvent objects (payload = 8B each)
    │
    ▼
  HeaderModel.headerBytes(mode)
    ├─ traditional → 12B header
    └─ compact     →  8B header
    ▼
  FootprintCalculator.bytesPerEvent()
    │ traditional: 12 + 8 = 20 → align → 24B
    │ compact:      8 + 8 = 16 → align → 16B
    ▼
  totalBytes(100M, mode)
    │ traditional = 2288 MB
    │ compact     = 1525 MB
    ▼
  savingPercent = (2288 − 1525) / 2288 = 33.3%
    │
    ├──→ heap footprint: −33%
    └──→ per-GC bytes copied: −33%  → shorter young-gen pauses
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Every object on the Java heap starts with a header that the JVM owns, before any of my own fields. That header has a mark word, which holds the identity hash code, the locking state, and the garbage-collection age bits, and a class pointer that tells the JVM what type the object is. On a sixty-four-bit JVM that header is traditionally twelve bytes with compressed class pointers, or sixteen bytes without, and it is paid once on every single object. Compact Object Headers, delivered as JEP 519 and made a supported product feature in Java 25, fold the class information into the mark word so the whole header shrinks toward eight bytes, enabled with the UseCompactObjectHeaders flag.

The reason this matters is entirely about allocation-heavy workloads dominated by many small objects. For a big array the header is a rounding error, but for a service that creates billions of tiny objects, the fixed header can be larger than the actual business data in each object. Trimming the header from sixteen bytes toward eight directly shrinks every one of those objects, and across billions of them that is a real double-digit percentage reduction in the live set.

In a project at National Bank of India we ran a transaction-enrichment pipeline that created one small event object per card swipe, hundreds of millions per day, and the service was spending too much time in young-generation garbage collection even though each event held only a few bytes of real data. The header was dominating the footprint. With compact headers each event dropped from twenty-four bytes to sixteen bytes, roughly a third smaller, and because a copying collector physically moves live objects, the collector had a third fewer bytes to copy on every minor collection. That translated into shorter pauses, less memory bandwidth, and higher sustainable swipe throughput on the same heap size.

The nuance I always add is that the win is workload-dependent and must be measured, not assumed. I confirm the real object layout with a tool like JOL rather than trusting a mental model, I verify that features relying on the mark word such as identity hashing and locking still behave correctly, and I expect large savings only where objects are genuinely small. So my summary is that Compact Object Headers reduce both heap footprint and garbage-collection copy cost by making every object smaller, and they pay off most exactly where a service allocates enormous numbers of tiny objects, which is precisely the kind of fine-grained event and cache workload common in banking pipelines.

---

keyPoints: JEP 519 (Java 25): reduces object header from 12-16 bytes to 8 bytes
Significant heap savings for applications with many small objects
Reduces memory footprint by 10-20% for typical applications
Combines mark word and class pointer into a single 64-bit header
